                                     PROJECT NO. 58481

 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                         §      PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                      §
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561                   §                   OF TEXAS

                           ELECTRIC HYDROGEN CO.
                       COMMENTS ON PROPOSED 16 TAC §25.194


       COMES NOW Electric Hydrogen Co. (EH2) and files these comments regarding

Commission Staff's Proposal for Publication (PFP) of new 16 Texas Administrative Code (TAC)

§25.194 relating to Large Load Interconnection Standards, which would set forth the standards

and criteria for an electric utility to interconnect a large load customer to the ERCOT transmission

network.

                                        BACKGROUND

       EH2 is an American manufacturing company that was founded in 2020 with a mission to

make electrolysis in the United States a viable cost competitive option for efficiently producing

hydrogen as a feedstock in industrial applications like refining, chemicals, and ammonia

fertilizer production. Over the past five years, EH2 has built a company that is economically

viable and contributing to the U.S. energy dominance agenda by producing fuel for domestic

consumption and export.

       EH2 manufactures electrolyzer systems at plants in Texas and Massachusetts. As demand

grows, it will need to build new facilities to meet that demand. EH2 also supports other domestic

manufacturing as it produces equipment needed for production from US-based manufacturers.

By doing so, the project on shores critical manufacturing jobs.

       EH2 has raised over $700 million in private capital; pioneered the most powerful, lowest-

cost electrolyzer plant in the world; built a 1.2 GW capacity factory here in the US; grown to
 more than 200 US employees; developed a pipeline of A-list announced customers like Uniper

and HIF; and constructed our first commercial installation for Infinium in Pecos, Texas. In Pecos,

Infinium uses EH2’s systems to produce hydrogen, which it then combines with CO2. Offtake

for the project is contracted to American Airlines and International Airlines Group—the parent of

British Airways.

       In addition to domestic demand for hydrogen, there is strong and growing global demand

for electrolytic hydrogen and its derivatives. Fuel suppliers are expanding their sales of

hydrogen-derived fuels in high-paying markets like Europe and Asia, and fertilizer producers

around the world are demanding domestic sources of ammonia, which can be made more cost

effectively with locally produced electrolytic hydrogen. These market opportunities are driving

Chinese manufacturers to ramp up production of electrolyzers to meet demand. EH2 is the only

domestic manufacturer that can counter Chinese influence on these markets in Latin America, the

Middle East, Asia, and Europe by directly competing with Chinese manufacturers on cost. EH2

has already met the cost metrics that China announced it will achieve in coming years. EH2’s

success means less reliance on Chinese technology here is the United States and more US-made

electrolyzer equipment sold abroad.

       In addition to manufacturing heavy equipment, EH2 develops hydrogen production

projects in the United States and is currently developing several projects in Texas. Its most

advanced project is located in Mont Belvieu, Texas. We are in late-stage negotiations to sell the

hydrogen from the Mont Belvieu project to a large Oil & Gas player that intends to use the

hydrogen to produce fuels for export to Europe, where demand for US fuels is growing. The rules

and processes under consideration in this docket are critical to ensure traditional industrial projects

like our hydrogen projects still have a reasonable path to commercialization.
                                           COMMENTS

   1. Well, established historical projects which complete the traditional interconnection

       process should not be forced to restart under a new paradigm.

       Our Mont Belvieu project entered the load queue in 2023 and as of the end of May 2026

has now completed two rounds of full interconnection studies and is preparing to enter into the

interconnection agreement with our TSP to complete the traditional process. After years of

development, it would be unjust to require historical projects, like the Mont Belview project, to

start over with new studies, extended timelines, and unplanned burdensome financial obligations.

       Projects that have completed their interconnection studies and interconnection agreement

processes by the date of the enactment of the relevant rules should be allowed to remain as Base

Load. It is inappropriate to retroactively apply new criteria that could not have been known or

anticipated when development began, to advanced stage projects, including payment of new

interconnection fees, new rules for financial refundability, new standards for study validity, and

elevated requirements for site control in this determination.

       If the Commission does not revert to applying historical process rules to all late stage

projects that have completed interconnection studies by the date of rule enactment (for purposes

of determining Base Load Qualification), at a minimum the March 4 deadline for testing study

validity should be moved out much closer to the date of rule adoption, and/or the TSP should be

empowered with more discretion to determine study validity achievement for individual projects

based on their assessment of impact.



   2. The financial burdens of the new rules are excessive, particularly for traditional

       industrial projects, and should move to a more reasonable position.
        We appreciate that the interconnection fee has been reduced from $100,000/MW to

$50,000/MW. While these fees may be palatable to some growth industries, they compromise the

competitiveness of traditional industrial projects which typically have low, infrastructure-style

returns. Industrial projects create good paying jobs in this State. If Texas were to lose its

attractiveness for industrial growth, the impact on jobs and the economy will be widely felt.

Developers of these types of projects rely on a conventional path to raise capital, which means

they only get progressed if there is a reasonably low amount of capital at risk before reaching final

investment decision (“FID”). Because offtake agreements, permits, and other development steps

are at risk in parallel with the grid interconnection process, developers cannot make significant at-

risk investments in the interconnection process at the stage of project development being proposed

under the new rules. Requiring material financial exposures prior to FID, while these other risks

remain, would require changes in how projects of these types are funded. Absent finding new

sources of risk tolerant capital, the early-stage non-refundable deposit requirements are likely to

become a material barrier to entry that will adversely impact industrial project growth in ERCOT.

It is critical that the Commission find a path that continues to present a reasonable risk pathway

for traditional industrial development in Texas.

       Similarly, CIAC payments have typically been negotiated between developers and TSPs to

ensure TSPs are fully funded for work they need to do to make the developer’s requested

energization schedule. In many cases this includes deferring initial deposits until work needs to

begin and spreading deposits into multiple installments that better reflect the spend curve. Lastly,

traditionally if a project failed, the TSP was fully funded but returned any unutilized funds to the

developer. The proposed rules requiring 100% of CIAC to be paid on the day of the interconnection
 agreement, regardless of the actual work schedule, and being fully non-refundable, is unjust and

unnecessary.

        A typical industrial facility such as ours requires on the order of $5 million of development

costs to reach FID. Taken together, if unchanged from current drafts, the two proposed rules

described above would add on the order of $20 million of additional cost to the Mont Belvieu

project before FID is even reached – a whopping 400% increase in the cost of doing business. It is

easy to see how this would present a meaningful barrier to industrial development and push

traditional industry to consider other states.

        We recommend further lowering the interconnection fee amount, allowing it to be credited

towards any CIAC payments, and allowing staged refundability consistent with typical

development project milestones (with a meaningful portion still refundable if development fails

prior to start of construction or FID). We believe this can be accomplished, allow a more reasonable

path for traditional industrial projects to thrive, while still setting the bar high enough to discourage

speculative projects.



    3. The proposed standards for real estate control financial burdens of the new rules are

        excessive, particularly for traditional industrial projects, and should move to a more

        reasonable position.

        Finally, the proposed rules would potentially require owning or leasing the project site as

a requirement for qualification for Base Load. We understand the intention here to present another

bar to speculative project, but this position compounds the concerns in the prior paragraph, and

worse yet, is detrimental to the interest of the landowner.
        It is conventional in industrial project development to control land via an option to

purchase, under which the development makes meaningful option payments to the landowner in

return for the unilateral option to close on the purchase of the property. The landowner continues

to enjoy the use of the land until the developer is ready to start construction, at which time they

close on the option and purchase the property.

       Even for a late stage project such as ours, FID could still be later in 2026, and forcing the

developer to purchase the property prior to the date on which construction would actually begin

simply adds more risk money (in our case, nearly another 100% in development costs) and is

detrimental to the landowner who can no longer continue to enjoy the property, despite it not yet

being needed for construction. This proposed rule is misguided, and an option to purchase should

be recognized as valid evidence of site control for both intermediate agreements and full

interconnection agreements, as well as for Base Load status purposes.



                                        CONCLUSION

       EH2 appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments and encourages the

Commission to move to formal publication of a proposed rule with modifications consistent with

these comments, in a way that can continue to show Texas’s leadership in attractive traditional

industrial development.
 Respectfully submitted,

/s/ Chris Shugart


                                           Chris Shugart
                   Vice President, Project Development
                                 Electric Hydrogen Co.
               4200 San Jacinto St., Houston, TX 77004
                                        (713) 822-5881
                                     cshugart@eh2.com
